week_8_requirement_this_supports: Requirement 4: apply exactly ONE mitigation to a named failure mode from the Week-8 zoo, and report that mode's count before -> after plus the measured price (added latency, tokens, or cost per claim).
honest_scope_note: This is a single-claim demonstration (CLM-2001), found and fixed live while re-verifying the merged agent BEFORE running the formal 10-claim trajectory-eval race. It is not yet the full-10-claim before/after count the rubric asks for - that still requires running scripts/race.py --suite triage over all 10 claims and scoring with trajectory_eval.py. This file shows the mitigation is real and already measured on the one case that exposed it; the full-sample count is a follow-up step, not fabricated here.

failure_mode.name: unresolved
failure_mode.definition: classify_failure_mode() in app/services/trajectory_eval.py tags any trace whose stopped_reason != 'finished' as unresolved - the agent hit a budget or a hard error before ever reaching a decision, regardless of whether its internal reasoning was actually correct.
failure_mode.why_this_one: Live-observed on CLM-2001: the agent correctly computed the right payout via compute_payout, then hit token_limit before it could call finish - a real, reportable trajectory failure even though the underlying reasoning was sound.

mitigation.one_line: ClaimAgent.run() now picks a job-specific system prompt and tool subset (via the same CLM-\d+ regex FixedClaimWorkflow already used), instead of sending both jobs' full prompt and all 11 tool schemas on every call.
mitigation.category: tighter tool description / reduced tool surface (one of the five listed mitigation types: tighter tool description, argument validation, hard step limit, re-planning, replace with workflow)
mitigation.not_a_hard_step_limit: DEFAULT_MAX_ITERATIONS/MAX_TOKENS were not changed - this mitigation reduces per-call overhead, it does not raise or lower any budget.

before_after_count.note: 1/1 -> 0/1 on this claim. The rubric wants this same count across all 10 claims; pending the full race run.

price_paid.metric: tokens_used and latency_ms, same claim, same model, same budgets - the two numbers the rubric explicitly allows as "the price"
price_paid.honest_reading: The price is not negative (the fix did not make anything cheaper) - it's roughly break-even on tokens and worse on latency for this one run, because the fixed prompt/tool overhead was never the dominant cost for a triage input (only list_documents was excludable; triage already needs 10 of 11 tools). The mitigation is still worth its price: it's the difference between a run that reports a decision and one that silently runs out of budget with the right answer already computed and never told to anyone.
